name: Custom t-shirt business
blurb: Print custom t-shirts for teams, events and businesses, or sell your own designs
title: T Shirt Business: How to Start a Custom T-Shirt Business
description: How to start a custom t shirt business: how printing makes money, equipment and print-on-demand options, who it suits, copyright risks and how to test first.
h1: How to start a custom t-shirt business
answer: A custom t-shirt business prints shirts to order for teams, schools, events and companies, or sells its own designs. You can start with a heat press or a print-on-demand service and move to screen printing as orders grow, but the work is competitive on price and copyright problems in designs can end it quickly.

sections.h: How a t-shirt business makes money
body: Custom orders are usually priced per shirt, with lower prices per shirt for larger runs and set-up fees for screens or designs. Selling your own designs earns per item, often through print-on-demand services that print and ship for you.
Costs include blank shirts, inks, vinyl or transfers, equipment, misprints, shipping and platform fees. With print-on-demand you avoid equipment but keep a smaller share of each sale.

ul: A printing method: heat transfer vinyl, direct-to-film or sublimation transfers with a heat press, screen printing, or direct-to-garment printing. Each needs different gear and skills.
A reliable source of blank shirts in common sizes and colours.
Design software and the rights to every image, font and logo you print.
A way to take orders and payment, plus sample shirts to show customers.
Business registration, tax setup and any workspace rules where you live.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People with design skills or local team and event contacts
Anyone who dislikes selling to clubs and businesses
Makers happy to learn equipment by trial and error
People expecting their designs to sell without marketing
Those who can start in a spare room or garage
Anyone planning to print brand logos or characters they do not own

ul: Copyright and trademark: printing logos, characters or lyrics without permission can bring takedowns, account bans and legal claims, even if a customer asked for it.
Price competition from online printers and print-on-demand sellers.
Misprints and returns: a wrong size or colour run is a full loss.
Equipment bought too early, before orders justify it.
Platform dependence if you only sell through one marketplace.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Make sample shirts through a print-on-demand service or a local printer.
Offer to print for one local team, club or event at a fair price.
Ask three small businesses whether they buy branded shirts and how often.
List a few original designs on one marketplace and track views and sales.
Price a heat press setup only once you have repeat orders.
Choose a niche: local teams, events, businesses or your own designs.
Pick one printing method and learn it on sample shirts.
Write a clear price sheet with minimums, set-up fees and turnaround.
Collect deposits before ordering blanks for custom jobs.
Track orders, misprints and time per job, and adjust prices.

faq.q: Do I need my own printer to start a t-shirt business?
faq.a: No. Print-on-demand services or local print shops let you test designs and customers first. Buy equipment once order volume makes it pay.

faq.q: Which printing method is best for beginners?
faq.a: A heat press with vinyl or transfers is often the simplest start for small runs. Screen printing suits larger runs but takes more setup and practice.

faq.q: Can I print team logos or famous characters?
faq.a: Only with permission from the rights owner. Customers asking for it does not make it legal, and marketplaces remove infringing designs.
